newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia markets on roller-coaster after U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Asia markets on roller-coaster after U.S. election.

text.p: Asian markets on Thursday took awild morning ride on post-U.S. election euphoria, with Hong Kong hitting a record high and Tokyo surging 400 points in early trade before both bourses deflated for the noon close.
Tokyo continued its dive in the afternoon and Australia shrugged off the Dow to fall on a gloomy earnings outlook.

Other Asian markets continued a rally that began after Tuesday's re-election of a Democratic president and a Republican congress. The U.S. election news and a stable outlook for U.S. economic policy and interest rates drove the Dow Industrials up 96.53 points overnight to a record close of 6,177.71.
Hong Kong stocks ended the morning session slightly lower, giving up strong earlier gains, as investors took modest profits in anticipation of a possible consolidation on Wall Street, brokers said.
"Sentiment remains positive, but we are likely to see more hedging activity with the market at these new heights," said Sean Li, associate director of Amsteel Securities.
"Both Wall Street and the Hang Seng have reached new highs with little consolidation along the way," he said.
The Hang Seng Index lost 15.03 points to 12,760.44, after etching a record intra-day high of 12,898.30 in mid-morning.

Tokyo stocks also jumped in early morning trade on Thursday, inspired by the post-election jubiliation on Wall Street, brokers said. But the futures-led gains melted away by midday as buying momentum petered out, they said.
At midday, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 0.79 point to 20,992.31, off a high of 21,142.24. By 0039 GMT, the Nikkei was down 113.90 points or 0.54 percent at 20,877.62.
"The Nikkei average gained sharply on Wednesday and it's only natural that it takes a breather," Akishige Ishikura, Dai-ichi Securities analyst, said.
On Wednesday, the Nikkei had surged nearly 2 percent on the U.S. election news to close at just below 21,000.
The backdrop of a record-setting Dow and interest in local small-capitalisation issues bolstered Kuala Lumpur shares, which continued their gains in morning trading.
The Composite Index of 100 leading stocks was up 5.60 points to 1,184.69 at 0248 GMT.

The Jakarta Composite Index rose 1.06 percent to 593.59 points after 30 minutes of trading on Thursday on foreign buying of selected big-capitalised stocks and bank counters, brokers said. By 0320 GMT, the index was up 1.44 percent, or 8.47 points to 595.81 points.
Brokers said the sharp rise in the Dow Jones coupled with positive domestic inflation and trade figures had improved market sentiment.
Other Asian market rallied mainly on domestic news.

Local punters dominated the Philippine equities market in early trade, nudging the index beyond the 3,000 level, brokers said. The composite index trudged up 11.85 points, or 0.40 percent, to 3,010.28 after 30 minutes.
Seoul shares ended the morning session slightly higher after a tug-of-war between bargain hunters and profit-takers, brokers said. The stock index rose 3.78 points to 751.07 by midday.

Taiwan share prices slowed to a mixed trading at mid-session as investors became cautious after the index failed to rise sharply in early trade, brokers said. With 80 minutes left, the weighted index was up 8.20 points or 0.12 percent at 6,661.85.
In New Zealand, the NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 13.68 points higher at 2,338.89 after profit-takers moved in to topple the index from its 2,353.09 peak.

Australian shares were slightly weaker at the midsession as the market ignored the Dow's gain and focused instead on the gloomy earnings outlook for Australian companies. At 0120 GMT, the All Ordinaries index was down 2.3 points at 2,358.3.

The Singapore share market was slightly firmer in early morning trade, while Thai stocks posted strong gains of nearly 2 percent in early trading on active carryover buying by investors of blue chips, mainly finance counters, brokers said.

The dollar was clinging slightly above its day's low by midday in Tokyo after plunging more than a yen on comments from a Ministry of Finance official, which set off aggressive selling that was augmented by successive stop-loss orders.
The greenback fell from 113.80 yen at the start of Asian trade to a low of 112.20 yen before recovering slightly. At 0518 GMT, the dollar traded at 112.20/2.25 yen and 1.5043/48 marks.
